strengths: Addresses an important practical problem: maintaining character and scene consistency in long story visualization, including sequences of up to 100 frames.
The iterative global-reference formulation is intuitive, training-free at inference time, and compatible with pretrained diffusion/IP-Adapter components.
The paper compares against autoregressive, reference-image, and subject-consistent generation baselines, and includes quantitative results, qualitative examples, ablations, and human evaluation.

Results generally show improved character-similarity metrics, especially for the SDXL variant, while global embeddings make each attention operation scale more favorably than feature-level consistent self-attention.
weaknesses: The central computational-efficiency claim is misleadingly evaluated. The proposed default performs ten complete additional diffusion-generation rounds, but Figure 8 compares only the cost of a single image-generation pass and only the attention-related FLOPs. End-to-end latency, total FLOPs, memory, and throughput for producing a complete story are absent; the full method may be roughly an order of magnitude more expensive than one-pass baselines.

The long-story evaluation is too small and weakly specified: it uses only 20 GPT-4o-generated stories, with no detailed prompt-generation procedure, released split, repeated seeds, confidence intervals, or statistical tests. This makes the claimed superiority on the paper's main setting difficult to establish.

The principal consistency metrics can reward homogenization rather than narrative correctness. Indeed, additional iterations substantially increase aCCS and reduce aFID while CLIP-T deteriorates. There is no entity-, relation-, action-, temporal-, or diversity-aware evaluation demonstrating that changing events and character states remain correct across a story.

Claims about improved fine-grained interactions rely heavily on selected examples and an under-documented human study. The paper omits the number and background of raters, number of evaluated samples, assignment and blinding protocol, agreement, uncertainty, and significance testing.

Baseline comparisons are not fully controlled across backbone sizes and conditioning mechanisms. Several gains are attributable mainly to Story-AdapterXL, while the non-XL model is worse than StoryDiffusion on regular-story aCCS/aFID and worse than IP-Adapter on long-story aFID. No matched compute or matched backbone comparison isolates the contribution of iteration and GRCA.

The methodological novelty is limited: the approach largely performs repeated IP-Adapter-style conditioning using pooled embeddings from previously generated images. The paper provides neither theoretical justification nor analysis of convergence, error reinforcement, cross-frame contamination, or why undifferentiated global attention should preserve story chronology.

Reproducibility is insufficient. Important implementation details are ambiguous, including how pretrained projection and attention weights realize Equation 3 without training, how reference tokens retain frame identity or order, whether noise and seeds are shared across iterations, batching, exact backbone/checkpoint configurations, and the precise definitions and computation of aFID/aCCS.

Some conclusions overstate the evidence: selected qualitative panels do not establish avoidance of reference-image flaws, and the 100-frame result is presented without controlled quantitative analysis at different sequence lengths. The paper also lacks a meaningful limitations or ethical-impact discussion despite possible amplification of identity stereotypes, dataset bias, and copyright concerns.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: maintaining character and narrative consistency in very long story visualization.
The iterative global-reference idea is intuitive, and using compact CLIP image tokens offers a plausible way to condition on many frames without the attention cost of full spatial features.

weaknesses: The computational-efficiency claim is inadequately supported. Figure 8 measures only attention FLOPs for one image in one generation pass, while the default method performs ten complete diffusion-generation rounds for every story frame. No end-to-end runtime, total FLOPs, peak memory, or throughput comparison is reported; total inference cost may therefore be much higher than the baselines.

The claimed superiority is mixed. On long stories, Story-Adapter has worse aFID than the corresponding IP-Adapter for both model families. The non-XL version also trails StoryDiffusion in CLIP-T and every reported human-evaluation category. Several apparent gains are demonstrated only by Story-AdapterXL, making it difficult to separate the method's contribution from backbone differences.

The central interaction-quality claim is not convincingly evaluated. CLIP-T, aCCS, and aFID do not directly measure whether subjects perform the correct actions or participate in the correct relationships. The supporting evidence is mainly selected qualitative examples and an under-specified subjective rating.

The long-story benchmark contains only 20 GPT-4o-generated stories and is insufficiently documented. The prompts, generation procedure, selection criteria, and benchmark artifacts are not provided in the paper. There are no confidence intervals, multiple-seed results, or statistical tests, so robustness and generalization cannot be assessed.

The human evaluation omits essential information, including the number and background of raters, number of evaluated samples, assignment and randomization procedure, blinding, instructions, inter-rater agreement, and uncertainty or significance analysis.

Reported results contain unexplained inconsistencies. The default ten-iteration Story-AdapterXL result is 0.318/0.802/94.30 in Tables 2 and 3 but 0.306/0.840/91.35 in Table 6. Table 6 also marks aFID with an upward arrow despite lower values being preferred elsewhere. Such discrepancies undermine confidence in the empirical conclusions.

The ablations do not fully support the narrative: removing initialization improves aFID relative to the full method, fixed lambda=0.5 substantially improves aFID, and the trade-offs among consistency, diversity, and prompt adherence are not analyzed. There is also no study of sensitivity across stories, seeds, reference-token counts, or story lengths.

The method is described as training-free and plug-and-play, but it relies on pretrained IP-Adapter/IP-AdapterXL weights whose learned image-conditioning projections are central to GRCA. The paper does not clearly distinguish avoiding new training from applicability to an arbitrary pretrained diffusion model.

Important implementation details remain ambiguous, including the precise checkpoints and image encoder, spatial resolutions, noise/seed reuse between iterations, attention layers receiving GRCA, positional treatment of ordered frames, and exact evaluation preprocessing. This limits reproducibility.

Overall, the approach is plausible and potentially useful, but the novelty is incremental and the evaluation does not establish the strong efficiency, interaction-quality, or across-the-board superiority claims required for acceptance at a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and difficult problem: maintaining global consistency and detailed interactions in story visualization over sequences as long as 100 frames.

The iterative paradigm is intuitive and useful. Conditioning each round on compact embeddings of all frames provides global context while avoiding the severe per-pass memory growth of feature-level consistent self-attention.
The method requires no task-specific optimization beyond existing pretrained components and can be attached to both Stable Diffusion and SDXL variants.

The experimental section covers regular-length stories, newly curated 50- and 100-frame stories, subject-consistent generation, human judgments, computational analysis, and multiple ablations. Qualitative examples are extensive.

The strongest configuration, Story-AdapterXL, obtains promising results: it leads the reported CLIP-T and aCCS results on the long-story benchmark and receives the best human-evaluation scores across all five long-story criteria.

The iteration ablation identifies a meaningful tradeoff: additional iterations substantially improve consistency while gradually reducing text alignment, supporting the proposed refinement mechanism and motivating the selected stopping point.
weaknesses: The headline comparison is confounded by backbone capacity. The base Story-Adapter is worse than StoryDiffusion on all three regular-story metrics and on two of three long-story metrics; it is also rated below StoryDiffusion in every reported human-evaluation category. The favorable conclusions primarily rely on Story-AdapterXL, but the paper does not establish a rigorously backbone-matched StoryDiffusion comparison.

The claimed computational efficiency is not demonstrated end to end. Figure 8 measures FLOPs for one image-generation pass, whereas the default method performs ten complete refinement rounds over every story frame. Total runtime, total FLOPs, peak memory, and comparisons at matched output quality are missing; the complete method may be substantially more expensive despite GRCA's low per-pass overhead.

The long-story evaluation is small, consisting of only 20 GPT-4o-generated stories. The manuscript does not provide sufficient information about prompt construction, diversity, filtering, or public availability, making generalization and reproducibility difficult to assess.

The automatic metrics incompletely support the central claims. CLIP similarity is a weak measure of compositional interaction correctness, while aCCS and aFID are presented as semantic-consistency measures without enough definition or validation. No dedicated evaluation measures identity preservation for multiple recurring characters, temporal/narrative coherence, or relation accuracy.

The human evaluation lacks essential methodological details, including the number and demographics of raters, number of evaluated examples, sampling and assignment procedure, blinding, baseline ordering, inter-rater agreement, confidence intervals, and significance testing. Consequently, small score differences cannot be interpreted reliably.

The ablations do not fully isolate the proposed components. There is no comparison against simpler alternatives such as conditioning on a pooled embedding, a sampled subset of frames, nearest relevant frames, or repeatedly applying IP-Adapter with fixed references. Sensitivity to token count, story length, random seeds, and the weighting schedule is also limited.

The assertion that repeated conditioning improves fine-grained interactions remains mostly qualitative. Iteration simultaneously increases reference strength, so improvements cannot be cleanly attributed to repeated engagement with the text; indeed, CLIP-T deteriorates as iteration proceeds.

Important reproducibility details are missing, including exact backbone/checkpoint assignments for every baseline, inference seeds, hardware, wall-clock costs, prompt templates, and uncertainty over repeated runs. Algorithm 1 and the description of how pretrained IP-Adapter attention weights are reused are also too ambiguous for confident reimplementation.

The paper contains several presentation inconsistencies, such as the incorrect upward arrow for aFID in Table 6 and claims that Story-Adapter generally outperforms StoryDiffusion despite the base model's mixed or inferior results. Overall, the idea is promising, but the evaluation and efficiency evidence fall slightly short of the top-tier acceptance threshold.

GRCA is a practical training-free construction that reuses pretrained IP-Adapter components and compact global embeddings, allowing all frames to be referenced with substantially lower per-pass memory than feature-based consistent self-attention.

The paper contains useful ablations of global versus local reference aggregation, iteration count, initialization, and conditioning-weight schedules. It also reports computational cost and offers accelerated and ControlNet variants.
The qualitative results cover long sequences, multiple styles, emerging characters, and interaction-heavy scenes; several examples visibly improve identity consistency over autoregressive baselines.
weaknesses: The long-story benchmark is too small and insufficiently documented: it contains only 20 GPT-4o-generated stories, with no detailed release protocol, prompt-generation procedure, selection criteria, or uncertainty estimates. Results are reported for one fixed random seed, so robustness cannot be assessed.

The quantitative evaluation is not convincing enough for the central claims. aCCS rewards visual similarity and can favor homogenized frames, while the described aFID computes FID between a single reference crop and later crops, an unusual and statistically questionable use of FID. Sample counts, detection failures, confidence intervals, and significance tests are absent.

The claimed state-of-the-art advantage is overstated. On regular stories, the base Story-Iter trails StoryDiffusion on all three reported metrics; Story-IterXL's gains are mostly concentrated in aCCS, with negligible aFID improvement and slightly worse CLIP-T. On long stories, some competing methods achieve substantially better aFID, and the non-XL Story-Iter is not uniformly superior.

Fine-grained interaction generation is a central claim, but it is supported mainly by selected qualitative examples and an under-specified human study. The paper omits the number and demographics of raters, evaluated samples, blinding/randomization protocol, inter-rater agreement, confidence intervals, and statistical testing. Table 8 also labels both final long-story rows as Story-Iter, apparently omitting the XL designation.

The technical novelty is moderate: GRCA largely concatenates projected CLIP image tokens and applies the pretrained IP-Adapter cross-attention repeatedly. Claims that embedding distributions converge, irrelevant history is adaptively forgotten, and defects are avoided are not formally justified or directly measured.

The method is expensive: the principal model requires ten complete regeneration rounds, approximately 43 PFLOPs and 250 minutes for a 100-frame story. The fast variant is more practical but degrades all main metrics, including producing worse aFID than StoryDiffusion. Assertions that future samplers can reduce cost by roughly 50 times are speculative.

Reproducibility details remain incomplete despite the stated supplementary code: the pseudocode leaves frame/noise-loop behavior ambiguous, baseline backbone and resolution matching is not fully established, and no multi-seed variability or hyperparameter-selection protocol is reported.

The ethics statement merely asserts compliance and does not discuss misuse, copyright and provenance of generated benchmark content, representation biases, or consent and compensation procedures for the human evaluation.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: maintaining consistency over very long visual stories, including sequences of up to 100 frames.

The proposed iterative paradigm is intuitive and compatible with pretrained diffusion and IP-Adapter components without task-specific training. Using compact global embeddings also makes conditioning on many reference frames memory-feasible.
The paper includes comparisons across several method families, component and weighting ablations, efficiency measurements, human evaluation, and extensive qualitative examples.
The ablations provide some evidence that full-sequence GRCA and iterative refinement improve the reported consistency metrics over simpler reference-selection strategies.
weaknesses: The central state-of-the-art claim is overstated. On regular-length stories, the non-XL Story-Iter is worse than StoryDiffusion on all three reported metrics. Story-IterXL provides a clear aCCS gain, but its aFID advantage over StoryDiffusion is only 0.21 and its CLIP-T is slightly lower. On long stories, several baselines outperform it on individual metrics, and no uncertainty or significance analysis establishes that the small differences are reliable.

The evaluation metrics are problematic for the claimed contribution. aCCS can reward appearance collapse, while the described aFID computes FID between a reference crop and later crops of an object; FID is not statistically meaningful with a single reference sample and can be highly unstable for small per-object sample sets. Neither metric directly measures narrative coherence, identity preservation under appearance changes, or correctness of multi-character interactions.

The new long-story benchmark is only 20 GPT-4o-generated stories—ten at each length—with insufficient documentation of prompts, entity distributions, difficulty, filtering, annotations, or release details. Results use a single fixed seed and provide no confidence intervals, repeated-seed analysis, or per-story statistics, making the conclusions vulnerable to prompt and sampling variance.

The human evaluation lacks essential methodological information, including the number and qualifications of raters, number and selection of evaluated stories, randomization and blinding, assignment protocol, agreement, and statistical uncertainty. Table 8 also contains two rows both labeled Story-Iter in the long-story section, apparently obscuring which result corresponds to Story-IterXL.

The purported mechanism is insufficiently validated. Claims that embedding distributions converge, iterative prompting improves fine-grained interactions, and attention suppresses irrelevant or noisy references are supported mainly by selected visualizations and informal explanations. There is no quantitative convergence analysis, interaction-specific automatic evaluation, controlled test of error correction, or analysis of when self-conditioning instead reinforces mistakes and homogenizes frames.

Comparisons are not consistently controlled for backbone, resolution, sampling budget, or compute. Many headline gains come from the XL variant, while older baselines may use weaker backbones. The fast variant is not compared against equally accelerated baselines, and comparisons with proprietary systems are poorly reproducible.

The default method is extremely expensive: a 100-frame story requires ten external passes, 43 PFLOPs, and approximately 250 minutes. This is substantially slower than StoryDiffusion, while the fast variant sacrifices the reported quality gains. Assertions that efficiency is unlikely to be a limitation are therefore not supported by the presented results.

Reproducibility remains limited despite the pseudocode. Important details such as baseline-specific configurations, exact evaluation implementations and aggregation, long-story prompts, human-evaluation materials, and treatment of detection failures are missing or unclear. The algorithm notation is also ambiguous about whether noise is shared or resampled across frames and iterations.

The ethics statement is merely a commitment to the conference code and does not discuss the use of copyrighted characters and generated benchmark content, demographic or cultural bias, consent and attribution, or misuse risks associated with coherent character generation.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and practically relevant contribution: an external iterative refinement paradigm that conditions each frame on the complete previous story, addressing long-range consistency and newly introduced characters.

GRCA is a sensible training-free design that reuses pretrained IP-Adapter weights and compact global embeddings, allowing conditioning on up to 100 reference frames with substantially lower memory than feature-level consistent self-attention.

The evaluation is broad, covering regular and long stories, modern generation and editing baselines, multiple automatic metrics, human judgments, qualitative comparisons, efficiency measurements, and targeted ablations.

Results provide positive evidence for the main contribution: Story-IterXL achieves the strongest aCCS in both principal evaluations, competitive text alignment, and favorable human ratings. The 100-frame demonstrations are visually compelling.

Ablations examine global versus restricted reference aggregation, iterative refinement, initialization, weighting schedules, iteration count, and accelerated and pose-controlled variants. The consistency-alignment trade-off is also acknowledged.
The paper is generally clear, and the inclusion of pseudocode, implementation settings, computational costs, and a fast LCM variant improves its practical value.
weaknesses: The long-story benchmark is small—only 20 GPT-4o-generated stories—and its construction, diversity, annotation, public availability, and potential prompt-selection bias are insufficiently documented. No uncertainty estimates or results across random seeds are reported.

The human evaluation omits essential methodological details, including the number and background of raters, number and sampling of evaluated stories, randomization and blinding, inter-rater agreement, and statistical significance. Table 8 also appears to mislabel Story-IterXL as a second Story-Iter entry.

The definition of aFID is questionable or at least seriously underspecified: it is described as FID between a single reference crop and later crops, for which covariance estimation is degenerate. Both aFID and aCCS also depend on detector-selected crops, yet detection failures and metric robustness are not analyzed.

Some state-of-the-art claims are overstated. On long stories, Story-IterXL has worse aFID than FLUX.1.Kontext, IP-AdapterXL, and SEED-LLaMA, while its gains over StoryDiffusion in CLIP-T are very small. On regular stories, gains over StoryDiffusion are likewise modest on CLIP-T and aFID.

The method is conceptually useful but technically incremental, largely combining repeated generation with standard attention over projected CLIP embeddings using pretrained IP-Adapter parameters. Claims about convergence, soft forgetting, noise suppression, and improved fine-grained interactions are intuitive rather than formally or directly validated.

Several implementation details remain ambiguous: the equations do not clearly describe the claimed token merging, the pseudocode is difficult to follow, and reuse or resampling of noise across external iterations is not specified precisely.

The full method is computationally expensive: 100-frame generation takes 250 minutes and roughly twice the FLOPs of StoryDiffusion. The fast variant addresses runtime but loses quality on CLIP-T and aFID, so the efficiency-quality trade-off remains substantial.
